titulo: Mercado busca alívio após tombo e vence prazo de passaportes de Flávio
resumo_dia: Na manhã desta terça-feira, o mercado financeiro tenta se estabilizar após a B3 registrar o pior pregão em seis anos, com o dólar a R$ 5,40 e o acionamento do circuit breaker no dia anterior. Vence hoje o prazo de 24 horas fixado pelo ministro Alexandre de Moraes para que Flávio Bolsonaro entregue seus passaportes à Polícia Federal. Nos Estados Unidos, aliados de Donald Trump pressionam por retaliações contra o Brasil, enquanto o governo Lula mantém a postura de não responder a acusações sem provas. Em Teerã, delegações da Arábia Saudita, Turquia e Paquistão mantêm negociações para conter a crise no Golfo antes da eleição americana. No Rio, a UFRJ abre a Semana do Servidor com atenção redobrada aos impactos do dólar e do novo cenário político no orçamento das pesquisas.

notas.titulo: Mercado busca trégua após tombo histórico do Ibovespa
notas.texto: Após a queda de 13,88% no pregão de segunda-feira e o acionamento do circuit breaker, os índices futuros da B3 e os recibos de ações brasileiras em Nova York apontam para uma tentativa de acomodação na abertura desta terça-feira. O dólar à vista, que encerrou cotado a R$ 5,40 na maior alta diária em meses, opera sob cautela. Segundo a Exame e a Bloomberg Línea, operadores aguardam os próximos sinais da equipe de transição do presidente reeleito e declarações de dirigentes do Banco Central. O foco permanece na sustentabilidade fiscal e na indicação do futuro ministro da Fazenda, depois que Rafael Fonteles rejeitou especulações em torno de seu nome. A volatilidade internacional e as decisões de juros do Federal Reserve nesta quarta-feira também restringem o apetite a risco.
notas.por_que_importa: A estabilização do câmbio é decisiva para controlar pressões inflacionárias sobre combustíveis, medicamentos e importações de insumos científicos.

fontes.enfoque: abertura dos mercados e indicadores de alívio pós-tombo
texto_integral: Agenda do mercado: os investidores começam esta terça-feira, 27, tentando avaliar os desdobramentos da reeleição de Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva (PT) para os preços dos ativos (rstavila1/envato)
Publicado em 27 de outubro de 2026 às 05h30.

Depois de uma das sessões mais turbulentas da história recente do mercado financeiro brasileiro, os investidores começam esta terça-feira, 27, tentando avaliar os desdobramentos da reeleição de Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva (PT) para os preços dos ativos. O Ibovespa caiu 13,88% na segunda-feira, 26, na maior perda percentual desde março de 2020, enquanto o dólar disparou 8,21%, para R$ 5,4027, na maior alta diária desde 1999.

A reação refletiu a revisão das expectativas de parte do mercado após a vitória de Lula sobre Flávio Bolsonaro (PL) no segundo turno, realizado no domingo, 25. A preocupação com os rumos da política econômica e fiscal do país desencadeou uma onda de vendas de ações e uma busca por proteção no dólar.
A sessão também foi marcada pelo acionamento do circuit breaker da B3, que interrompeu as negociações por 30 minutos logo na abertura.

Nesta terça-feira, a atenção dos investidores se divide entre indicadores econômicos no Brasil e nos Estados Unidos, a agenda do Banco Central e os primeiros desdobramentos da reprecificação dos ativos após o resultado eleitoral.

A agenda brasileira começa às 8h, com a divulgação da Sondagem da Construção de outubro e do Índice Nacional de Custo da Construção — M (INCC-M), ambos pela Fundação Getulio Vargas (FGV). No levantamento anterior, a sondagem marcou 90,5 pontos, enquanto o INCC-M registrou alta de 0,25%.

Às 9h, o Instituto Brasileiro de Geografia e Estatística (IBGE) divulga o Índice de Preços ao Produtor das indústrias extrativas e de transformação referente a setembro. Os dados ajudam a acompanhar a evolução dos preços na indústria brasileira.

Nos Estados Unidos, os números começam a sair às 9h, com a atualização final das permissões para construção de moradias de setembro, divulgada pela Associação Nacional de Corretores de Imóveis (NAR). Em agosto, o indicador havia recuado 2,1% na comparação mensal.

Às 9h30, o mercado acompanha as encomendas de bens duráveis de setembro, divulgadas pelo Departamento do Censo americano. Em agosto, o indicador ficou estável em relação ao mês anterior. Os números ajudam a avaliar o ritmo da demanda por bens de maior valor e o desempenho da atividade industrial.

Dois indicadores saem às 11h: a confiança do consumidor americano de outubro, medida pelo Conference Board, e as vendas de novas moradias de setembro, divulgadas pela NAR. Em setembro, a confiança do consumidor estava em 81,9 pontos, enquanto as vendas de novas moradias haviam avançado 6,4% em agosto, na comparação mensal.

Os dados americanos entram no conjunto de informações acompanhado pelos investidores para avaliar a trajetória da economia e as perspectivas para a política monetária do Federal Reserve (Fed), o banco central dos Estados Unidos.

No Brasil, o presidente do Banco Central, Gabriel Galípolo, participa das 11h às 13h de uma entrevista coletiva sobre o Relatório de Estabilidade Financeira (REF), em Brasília. A apresentação será transmitida pelo canal do BC no YouTube.

O documento e as declarações da autoridade monetária estarão no radar dos investidores em um momento de forte volatilidade nos mercados brasileiros. A coletiva ocorre após a sessão de segunda-feira, quando a revisão das expectativas sobre a política econômica provocou perdas expressivas na bolsa e uma disparada do dólar.
Já o Conselho Nacional de Justiça (CNJ) discute uma proposta de resolução para criar a Política Nacional de Tratamento Adequado aos Precatórios no Poder Judiciário.

Nos Estados Unidos, o Tesouro realiza às 14h um leilão de títulos públicos de cinco anos, conhecidos como Treasury notes (T-notes). A operação integra a agenda de financiamento do governo americano e pode ser acompanhada pelos investidores interessados na demanda por títulos soberanos e no comportamento dos juros no mercado de renda fixa.

No Brasil, a Hypera também divulga seus resultados. Os números das companhias entram no radar dos investidores em uma sessão na qual a avaliação do cenário político e econômico deve continuar influenciando a precificação dos ativos.

texto_integral: Bloomberg Línea — A vitória de Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva nas eleições presidenciais do Brasil provocou uma forte correção nos mercados financeiros e revelou o risco que os investidores já haviam precificado antes do segundo turno.

O dólar subiu 8,63% em relação ao real, enquanto o Ibovespa caiu 13,88% na segunda-feira (26), depois que as expectativas do mercado de uma vitória de Flávio Bolsonaro e de uma mudança de rumo na política econômica foram frustradas.

Lula obteve 51,8% dos votos válidos contra 48,2% de Flávio Bolsonaro. O resultado surpreendeu os operadores, que haviam atribuído uma probabilidade próxima a 75% a uma vitória do candidato da oposição, segundo o JPMorgan (JPM).

Para a equipe do banco norte-americano, “o desempenho superior do Brasil dependia de uma mudança de política, mas acarretava um risco que os mercados já haviam descontado”, apesar de as pesquisas anteciparem uma disputa acirrada.
JPMorgan e Citi alertam sobre riscos

O JPMorgan considera que a permanência de Lula no poder reduz as perspectivas de uma transformação na política econômica, uma expectativa que havia sustentado sua decisão de elevar a recomendação sobre o Brasil para overweight em 5 de outubro.

O banco estima que as valorizações no mercado de ações possam recuar de um múltiplo de 9,7 vezes os lucros projetados para os próximos 12 meses para 8,3 vezes, podendo chegar até 7 vezes caso a deterioração das expectativas persista.

A pressão afetaria especialmente as empresas ligadas ao consumo interno, as pequenas empresas e aquelas com maior endividamento. Os exportadores, por outro lado, poderiam mostrar maior resistência diante da desvalorização do real.

O JPMorgan também alerta que “o ponto de partida fiscal se deteriorou acentuadamente durante a campanha”, tanto pelas medidas já adotadas quanto pelos novos compromissos eleitorais, o que representa uma dificuldade adicional para o próximo mandato de Lula.

Em relação à dívida soberana, os analistas do banco reduziram sua recomendação para o Brasil de overweight para underweight. A instituição considera que os spreads de crédito ainda oferecem margem para uma correção em relação a outros emissores com classificação BB.

Em moedas e taxas locais, o JPMorgan reduziu de overweight para “neutro” sua recomendação sobre o Brasil. Para os rendimentos da dívida local, prevê um cenário de queda de 15,5%, embora prefira aguardar antes de adotar uma posição mais defensiva.

No setor de crédito corporativo, o banco mantém sua recomendação de overweight dos títulos brasileiros com classificação de investimento, mas rebaixou a recomendação para underweight dos títulos de alto rendimento, diante de seu desempenho relativo recente e da deterioração das condições do mercado

André Mazini, analista do Citi (C), afirmou que “a vitória de Lula no segundo turno deve ser recebida negativamente pelo mercado, em nossa opinião, já que o resultado foi contrário às expectativas dos investidores”.
O banco identificou uma reação assimétrica entre os investidores: as perdas esperadas em caso de vitória de Lula superavam amplamente os ganhos previstos em caso de eventual vitória de Bolsonaro.
Para o UBS, a alta anterior dos ativos brasileiros baseava-se na expectativa de um governo favorável ao mercado e de um programa de consolidação fiscal rápido e contundente.
No entanto, o banco considera que ainda não há medidas concretas suficientes para justificar as valorizações alcançadas após o primeiro turno.

A instituição financeira prevê que as valorizações do Ibovespa retornem aos níveis anteriores ao primeiro turno eleitoral. O banco destaca que a bolsa estava sendo negociada a 9,6 vezes os lucros esperados, sem refletir plenamente os riscos fiscais.

No mercado de renda fixa, o UBS prevê que o rendimento real do título brasileiro indexado à inflação com vencimento em 2050 suba de 6,74% para pelo menos 7,10%. O banco também antecipa uma redução mais lenta da Selic caso o ajuste fiscal seja adiado.

O principal desafio para Lula será a situação das contas públicas. O UBS calcula que a dívida brasileira ultrapassa 80% do PIB, enquanto o déficit fiscal gira em torno de 10%, impulsionado em parte pelo elevado custo dos juros.
O banco estima que os compromissos de gastos anunciados durante a campanha somem cerca de R$ 300 bilhões, um fardo adicional para um governo que precisará recuperar a credibilidade orçamentária.

Para o UBS, a recuperação da confiança exige “um pacote concreto com medidas quantificadas, não apenas declarações de intenções”, além de compensar os compromissos de gastos eleitorais e obter a aprovação do Congresso antes do final do ano.

O Morgan Stanley (MS) também identifica riscos fiscais. Sua previsão aponta para um déficit primário de 0,7% do PIB em 2027 e uma dívida bruta equivalente a 86,9%, embora alerte que ambos os indicadores possam se deteriorar.

A instituição estima que mais de 91% dos gastos públicos brasileiros sejam obrigatórios, uma rigidez orçamentária que limita a capacidade do governo de conter as pressões fiscais sem reformas estruturais.

Entre os compromissos identificados estão R$ 22,7 bilhões adicionais para o Bolsa Família, R$ 5,2 bilhões em receitas menores devido à proibição das apostas digitais e R$ 5 bilhões para o Desenrola 3.0 ao longo de 2027.

O Morgan Stanley alerta que, em caso de um ajuste tardio e superficial, “a dívida bruta como porcentagem do PIB poderia atingir 106% em 2035”, de acordo com as simulações de seus economistas Thiago Machado e Ana Madeira.

Os estrategistas de mercado Nikolaj Lippmann, Julia Nogueira e Marcos Rios estimam seu cenário pessimista para o Ibovespa em 130.000 pontos em meados de 2027, o equivalente a 6,2 vezes os lucros esperados, “em um cenário de deterioração contínua da política fiscal”.

No mercado de taxas, Ioana Zamfir e Sofía Palacios prevêem “uma correção de pelo menos 300 pontos-base nas taxas DI, que deve ocorrer de forma escalonada”. Uma maior deterioração fiscal poderia levar o mercado a precificar novos aumentos da Selic.

Benito Berber, analista do Natixis, identificou a responsabilidade fiscal como a principal preocupação dos investidores. Em uma pesquisa realizada antes das eleições, 76% de seus clientes apontaram esse fator como sua maior preocupação.
A composição do Congresso também será determinante. Os partidos de centro-direita e direita ampliaram sua representação, o que pode dificultar a aprovação de iniciativas do Executivo.
A Natixis considera que as perspectivas do real dependerão das intervenções do Banco Central, das condições financeiras internacionais e dos anúncios fiscais do novo governo.
A Bloomberg Economics, no entanto, apresenta uma visão menos pessimista sobre as consequências econômicas da vitória de Lula.
Adriana Dupita e Jimena Zúñiga consideram que “há boas razões para esperar que a queda dos ativos brasileiros seja significativa, mas temporária”.

As economistas destacam que o Brasil mantém fundamentos capazes de limitar a deterioração: crescimento econômico positivo, inflação dentro da margem de tolerância, uma balança de pagamentos resistente e taxas de juros atraentes.

Elas também questionam se o resultado eleitoral, por si só, justifica uma mudança radical nas expectativas fiscais, já que ambos os candidatos fizeram promessas onerosas sem detalhar um caminho suficiente para o superávit.
A Bloomberg Economics prevê uma consolidação fiscal gradual e moderada, independentemente de quem tivesse vencido as eleições.

A atenção dos bancos se voltará agora para a nomeação do ministro da Fazenda, as primeiras medidas orçamentárias, a resposta do Congresso e as decisões do Banco Central, cuja próxima reunião está marcada para 4 de novembro.

notas.titulo: Vence prazo de 24 horas para Flávio Bolsonaro entregar passaportes
notas.texto: Termina nesta terça-feira a ordem do ministro Alexandre de Moraes, do STF, que intimou o senador Flávio Bolsonaro a entregar todos os seus passaportes à Polícia Federal. A decisão, tomada no âmbito de apurações sob sigilo ligadas a movimentações financeiras, proíbe o parlamentar de deixar o território nacional e veda contato com o advogado Willer Tomaz. Conforme noticiado pelo Estadão e pela RTP, a defesa do senador ingressa com pedidos de reconsideração, sustentando que a restrição viola prerrogativas parlamentares e foi baseada em declarações públicas de terceiros. A oposição articula levar o caso a comissões internacionais de direitos humanos, enquanto líderes partidários no Senado buscam evitar que o episódio paralise as votações regimentais da Casa nesta semana.
notas.por_que_importa: O cumprimento da medida cautelar sela a derrota eleitoral e redefine o comando da oposição no Congresso nos próximos meses.

fontes.enfoque: notificação da PF e estratégia jurídica da defesa
texto_integral: O Estadão relata que a Polícia Federal cumpriu intimação judicial que determina o recolhimento de todos os passaportes do senador Flávio Bolsonaro no prazo de 24 horas, além de impedi-lo de viajar ao exterior.

A medida, decretada pelo ministro Alexandre de Moraes, atinge documentos comuns e diplomáticos. A defesa do parlamentar sustenta que inexiste fundamentação jurídica para a cautelar e planeja recorrer ao plenário da corte.

notas.titulo: Ala trumpista prega retaliações e Planalto mantém silêncio institucional
notas.texto: Após o ex-presidente Donald Trump classificar o pleito brasileiro como suspeito em declarações à imprensa no dia anterior, operadores políticos de seu entorno, como Steve Bannon, passaram a defender sanções diplomáticas e tarifas seletivas contra o Brasil. Segundo a Folha de S.Paulo, o Palácio do Planalto e o Itamaraty confirmaram que não responderão a insinuações informais, tratando o processo eleitoral como assunto soberano referendado por dezenas de chefes de Estado. Diplomatas brasileiros destacam que mensagens formais de reconhecimento e votos de cooperação já foram transmitidos pelas principais chancelarias da União Europeia, Reino Unido e Japão, esvaziando tentativas de isolamento internacional durante o período de transição.

O governo do presidente Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva (PT) afirmou não estar preocupado com a declaração do presidente dos Estados Unidos, Donald Trump, de que o resultado das eleições brasileiras pareceu “fraudado”.
Fontes no Planalto e Itamaraty avaliam que a fala não terá consequências e não exige uma reação neste momento, conforme apurou o SBT News.

Lula foi reeleito no domingo (25), com uma vantagem de aproximadamente 4,4 milhões de votos sobre Flávio Bolsonaro (PL), candidato apoiado pelo presidente norte-americano e pelo secretário de Estado dos EUA, Marco Rubio.
Acompanhe o SBT News nas TVs por assinatura Claro (586), Vivo (576), Sky (580) e Oi (175), via streaming pelo +SBT,Site e YouTube, além dos canais nas Smart TVs Samsung, LG e Roku.
Somente na tarde desta segunda (26), Trump comentou a eleição brasileira e declarou:
+ Os telefonemas de ministros por trás da decisão de Zanin

O governo brasileiro não pretende se manifestar publicamente sobre o episódio, a menos que haja uma nova investida de Trump. A avaliação é de que a declaração pode ser resultado de uma pressão do Departamento de Estado norte-americano, como ocorreu em outras ocasiões, mas não deve produzir efeitos concretos.

Também na avaliação do governo, Trump costuma questionar a legitimidade de resultados eleitorais com os quais não concorda, classificando-os como fraudados. Por isso, o Planalto pretende ignorar a declaração e não dar ao presidente norte-americano a atenção que ele busca.

O governo destaca ainda que o resultado das eleições já foi reconhecido por manifestações de diversos líderes internacionais. Nesta segunda-feira (26), Lula conversou por telefone com a presidente do México.
+ PL reconhece vitória de Lula sobre Flávio
Mais cedo, o vice-presidente Geraldo Alckmin comentou a fala de Trump em uma entrevista à Rede Vanguarda, classificando-a como equivocada.

“Olha, totalmente equivocada, né? Primeiro não se interfere na política de outro país. Essa é uma regra basilar. Segundo não tem nenhum referencial pra dizer isso. Aliás, o Brasil é um exemplo pro mundo. De urna eletrônica, de segurança jurídica. Democracia é assim. Você ganha eleição, você perde a eleição, é o povo que decide", disse Alckmin.

No domingo (25), o presidente brasileiro recebeu cumprimentos de chefes de Estado e de governo de países como Uruguai, Paraguai, Chile, Equador, Guiana, Peru, Guatemala, República Dominicana e Bolívia.

Lula também foi parabenizado pelo presidente do Conselho Europeu, António Costa, pelo primeiro-ministro do Canadá, Mark Carney, pela primeira-ministra do Japão, Sanae Takaichi, e pelo presidente da Rússia, Vladimir Putin. A presidente da Comissão Europeia, Ursula von der Leyen, também está entre as lideranças internacionais que cumprimentaram Lula.
Há pelo menos 10 outros líderes internacionais interessados em conversar por telefone com o presidente brasileiro.

notas.titulo: Teerã aceita novas rodadas de diálogo com potências regionais
notas.texto: Negociadores do Irã concordaram em prosseguir as reuniões diplomáticas em Teerã com delegações da Arábia Saudita, Turquia e Paquistão, informou a CBS News nesta manhã. As conversas, intermediadas pelo Catar e acompanhadas por observadores internacionais, buscam conter uma escalada armada e negociar a reabertura segura das rotas comerciais no Estreito de Ormuz. Diplomatas árabes avaliam o encontro como um canal derradeiro de contenção antes de eventuais ordens militares de Washington, que mantém contingente em prontidão. Em troca de trégua na navegação, o governo iraniano exige a suspensão dos embargos a terminais petrolíferos e garantias contra ataques preemptivos às suas instalações nucleares.
notas.por_que_importa: O andamento dessas negociações dita o preço do barril de petróleo no mercado internacional e o custo global do frete marítimo.

texto_integral: Follow updates on the war in the Middle East for Monday, October 28, here. See earlier developments below.
The cost of the Iran war has risen to an estimated $47 billion, according to an estimate from the U.S. military's Central Command obtained by CBS News Tuesday.
Like previous estimates, it does not include damage to U.S. military bases in the Middle East. The bulk of the cost, $29 billion, is for replacing expended munitions.
According to a report released by the nonpartisan Congressional Budget Office in September, the Iran war could cost approximately $2 billion to $3 billion per month for as long as it continues.

Exit polls from Israel's major television networks project that a majority of Israelis voted against Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu's coalition in Tuesday's election, but his Likud party still emerged as the largest party among all the contenders. Neither bloc, Netanyahu or the opposition, has a clear majority.
While Netanyahu appears to have won fewer votes than his main challenger, according to the early exit polls, both candidates will likely struggle to cobble together a coalition.
One or the other would need to obtain majority support in Israel's 120-seat parliament, known as the Knesset, in order to form a government.

Israel's two Arab parties won more seats in parliament than in any previous election. That electoral success comes after what some Arab voters told CBS News was a difficult time for them in the country under the hard-right government of Netanyahu, prompting a historic turnout for the minority community.

Both Netanyahu and those opposing him have vowed not to form a government reliant on Arab parties, arguing it would endanger the country if they gain enough seats to influence Israel's engagement in its myriad conflicts. Arab citizens of Israel are around 20% of the population.

International Atomic Energy Agency chief Rafael Grossi urged Iran during a U.N. Security Council meeting on Tuesday to grant immediate access to his agency so it can verify the Islamic republic's nuclear materials.
The IAEA has not had access to key nuclear facilities in Iran since Israel and the United States launched strikes on nuclear sites in June 2025.
Nuclear facilities have also been hit in the latest war, and the IAEA has repeatedly called for access.

"I invite Iran to work with the IAEA without any further delay to clarify outstanding safeguards questions and to give the IAEA the information and access the agency requires, so that it can verify all relevant facilities and material, as is Iran's legal obligation," Grossi said.
The Security Council meeting followed a resolution passed by the IAEA board last month that referred Iran to the top U.N. body over its nuclear "non-compliance."

The resolution, submitted by Britain, France, Germany and the United States, marks the first time Iran has been referred to the Security Council in 20 years for failing to comply with its nuclear reporting obligations.
The move has been seen as largely symbolic as China and Russia hold power to veto any sanctions against their ally Tehran. Both countries were joined by Niger in voting against the IAEA resolution.

Nearly 100 fighters have been killed in renewed clashes between Yemen's Iran-backed Houthis and Saudi-backed government forces in southwestern Yemen, military sources from both sides told the AFP news agency on Tuesday.
At least 63 Houthi fighters and 34 pro-government combatants have died, mostly near the Bab el-Mandeb Strait, the Red Sea's strategic southern chokepoint, they said.
The clashes, which began with airstrikes late on Monday, are the fiercest since the Houthis seized swathes of territory from the Saudi-backed government in a lightning offensive last month.

The Houthis fought off "an attempted advance by Saudi enemy forces ... from the southern direction of Bab al-Mandab," military spokesman Yahya Saree posted on X, describing "a large number of dead and wounded."
The Houthi military sources said Saudi Arabia carried out dozens of airstrikes, hitting Mayyun Island in the strait as well as Dhubab and Mocha further up the Red Sea coast.
Government military sources said intense fighting was under way in the Bab el-Mandeb area, claiming they had made progress on the ground.
Earlier this month, Yemen's government launched a counteroffensive with Saudi air support to try to reclaim the territory lost to the Houthis.
But the campaign has faltered, while the Houthis have ramped up deadly attacks on Saudi Arabia that shuttered its capital's airport for two weeks and disrupted daily life.
Riyadh leads a military coalition that first intervened in the conflict in 2015. The fighting has devastated Yemen and created one of the world's worst humanitarian crises.

Russian President Vladimir Putin and his Iranian counterpart, President Masoud Pezeshkian, discussed working together on oil and gas projects as the two met in person at the Gas Exporting Countries Forum Summit in Moscow on Tuesday.
The two leaders "discussed expanding political, economic, trade and energy cooperation, including joint projects in the oil and gas sectors," according to a readout from the Iranian government.

Pezeshkian also discussed working together on natural gas exports. Iran ranks third in the world in natural gas production — 280 billion cubic meters per year, according to the president — behind only the U.S. and Russia.

"Pezeshkian emphasized that global developments necessitate joint technical-engineering cooperation and strategic governance across international energy markets," the government said, presumably referring to the war with the U.S.
Russia and Iran have worked together for years. As the war in Ukraine continues, Russia continues to purchase Shahed drones for use in attacks.

The two countries have rarely coordinated on energy projects, however, as both countries produce massive amounts of crude on their own. The timing of the discussion Tuesday in Russia is especially important though because Iran has been cut off from importing or exporting crude due to the U.S. blockade on Iranian ports.

France's deputy chief of mission in Tehran was this month subjected to "intimidation by individuals claiming to belong to the Iranian security forces," a diplomatic source told the AFP news agency on Tuesday.
The incident, the second involving French diplomats in Tehran in less than four months, highlights the sharp deterioration in relations between France and Iran.

In response to the mistreatment of the diplomat in early October, Iran's ambassador to France was summoned by the French foreign ministry, the source said, without specifying the exact date of the summons.
"He was reminded in the strongest terms that we expect the Iranian authorities to take all necessary measures to guarantee the security of our personnel and premises," the source said.

French magazine Le Point, which first reported the incident, said the diplomat was forcibly stopped in the street by members of Iran's security forces, in breach of his diplomatic status. The encounter culminated in what the magazine described as a forceful interrogation.
The episode follows a July incident involving two French diplomats based in Tehran.
French Foreign Minister Jean-Noel Barrot accused the Iranian authorities at the time of having "detained them without reason for several hours," adding one of them had been "physically manhandled."

Iran said at the time the diplomats had been "briefly questioned" by security services after attending a "meeting with several individuals wanted by the authorities," and denounced French "interference … under the pretext of engaging with civil society."

The Iran-backed Houthis claimed Thursday that they struck three different airports in southwestern Saudi Arabia, and repelled an advance by Saudi-affiliated forces from the southern direction of the Bab el-Mandeb Strait.

Houthi military spokesperson Brig. Gen. Yahya Saree said on X that the group's forces had "succeeded in targeting two military transport aircraft with two ballistic missiles: the first at Najran Airport and the second at King Khalid Air Base in Khamis Mushait," both of which are in southwestern Saudi Arabia.
"Both operations successfully achieved their objectives, by the grace of God," he added.

In a separate statement on X, Saree said Houthi forces earlier thwarted an attempted advance by what he described as Saudi enemy forces "from the southern direction of Bab al-Mandab," the gateway to the Red Sea.
"These force concentrations were targeted with a number of ballistic missiles and heavy weapons, resulting in large numbers of dead and wounded," he said.
In a third statement Tuesday, Saree claimed the Houthis had struck Abha International Airport, also in the Saudi southwest.
"The strike was accurate and led to the disruption of air traffic at the airport," he said.
An oil tanker has caught fire after being caught in the Strait of Hormuz, Iran's navy said on Tuesday.

"Hours ago, a rogue oil tanker that had switched off its tracking systems and was attempting to pass through a prohibited and unsafe area east of the Strait of Hormuz struck naval mines, sustaining damage and catching fire," the navy's public relations office said.
"The Strait of Hormuz is unsafe and closed to rogue ships and vessels attempting to pass through without coordination," it added.

Iran has repeatedly said it will only allow vessels to pass through the waterway if they coordinate with authorities. The U.S. has urged shippers to use a southern route through the strait that Tehran regards as illegal.
Iranian Parliament Speaker Mohammad Bagher Ghalibaf said Supreme Leader Mojtaba Khamenei is in "perfect health," describing him as energetic, hopeful and composed following a meeting.
Khamenei was seriously wounded in the strikes that killed his father, Ali Khamenei, sources told CBS News in March. He has not been seen in public since the start of the war.
"The leader is in perfect health, and truly, what I observed during the meeting was a strong, energetic, hopeful and resolute spirit, along with inner peace," Ghalibaf said Tuesday.
"These qualities were fully evident in the leader," he added, "and I felt with all my being that this resolve and inner peace reflect a strong faith in Almighty God and a deep belief in the people."
The Saudi-led coalition fighting against Yemen's Iran-backed Houthis said Tuesday they had downed two ballistic missiles targeting Riyadh, the Saudi capital.
"Saudi air defenses intercepted and destroyed two ballistic missiles launched by the Houthi group toward the capital, Riyadh," spokesperson Maj. Gen. Turki Al-Malki wrote in a post on X.
Multiple explosions were heard in Riyadh on Tuesday, journalists from the AFP news agency said.
Residents received a text-message alert on their mobile phones warning of an "aerial threat" and instructing them to seek shelter.
This latest attack follows weeks of strikes by the Houthis, who claimed Tuesday to have struck a refinery in eastern Saudi Arabia.

A Kuwaiti State Security and Terrorism Criminal Court sentenced three men to death on Monday over an alleged plot to assassinate First Deputy Prime Minister and Interior Minister Sheikh Fahad Al-Yousef, with prosecutors accusing the defendants of spying for Iran, communicating with Iranian-linked entities and joining Hezbollah, two judicial sources told the AFP news agency Tuesday.
The court also sentenced eight other defendants to varying prison terms.

Those sentenced to death included cleric and National Islamic Alliance Secretary-General Hussein Abdullah Al-Maatouq and two other men. One of the defendants had previously been convicted of terrorism in 2016 and later received a pardon before being arrested again in April, the sources said.

According to Kuwaiti newspaper Al-Rai, the defendants were accused of communicating with Iran and entities allegedly operating in its interests, including Lebanese group Hezbollah, to carry out hostile acts against Kuwait following the killing of Iran's Supreme Leader Ali Khamenei on Feb. 28, at the beginning of the U.S.-Israeli war against Iran.

The defendants were also accused of joining Hezbollah, a banned group in Kuwait, while knowing its objectives, and of engaging in activities allegedly intended to undermine the country's political, social and economic order and harm its national interests.

Kuwaiti newspaper Al-Qabas reported prosecutors accused the defendants of attempting to use explosives to carry out the alleged assassination plot and spread panic. One defendant was separately accused of attempting to bring explosives into the country to enable the others to carry out the alleged operation.

The reported Iran connection forms a central part of the case, although the allegations against the defendants do not, on their own, establish that the Iranian government directed the alleged assassination plot.
Yemen's Iran-backed Houthis claimed Tuesday to have struck a refinery in eastern Saudi Arabia.

"With the help of Almighty God, the Yemeni Armed Forces succeeded in targeting the Ras Tanura refinery in the Eastern Province with a ballistic missile," military spokesperson Brig. Gen. Yahya Saree said in a post on X.
"The strike was accurate," he added, "and caused massive fires at the targeted site."
The alleged strike follows weeks of Houthi attacks against the world's top exporter of crude oil.
A resident in the nearby city of Al Khobar told the AFP news agency he heard explosions around dawn and then received a warning message on his phone.
"We got the alert on the mobile and then heard a very loud bang," the resident said.
The Ras Tanura facility along Saudi Arabia's eastern Gulf coast is home to one of the largest refineries in the Middle East and is a cornerstone of the kingdom's energy sector.

The complex has a capacity to refine 550,000 barrels per day. It has been repeatedly targeted by Iranian strikes, including a drone attack in early March that forced a partial shutdown of the refinery.

London — Two men have been charged with serious security offenses in Britain after being arrested in connection with the incident last month near RAF Fairford, the air base in England that had been used by the U.S. military to launch strikes on Iran, the U.K. Crown Prosecution Service (CPS) said Tuesday.
Mohmed Abdulkarim, 24, and Nouman Essghir, 24, both British nationals and London residents, were charged under the 2023 National Security Act.

Abdulkarim was charged with "assisting a foreign intelligence service" in September and "engaging in conduct that was likely to materially assist a foreign intelligence service in carrying out U.K.-related activities."

The CPS said Essghir was charged with a national security offense after he "approached or was in the vicinity of a prohibited place and his conduct was for a purpose that he knew, or having regards to other matters known to him ought reasonably to have known, was prejudicial to the safety or interests of the United Kingdom."
Both men were arrested last week on suspicion of assisting Iran's intelligence service in a suspected plot targeting the Fairford air base in England.
The U.S. embassy in Baghdad has shot down two drones, Saudi state television channel Al-Arabiya reported Tuesday.
An Iraqi security source told the outlet that air defenses protecting the embassy destroyed the drones.

The government-owned Iraqi television channel Al-Anbar reported that the head of Iraq's Security Media Cell, Saad Maan, said that explosions heard across the capital were the result of a drone being intercepted and shot down.
The drone's origin remains unknown, and no immediate reports of casualties or damage have been released. The U.S. State Department has not yet commented on the incident.
An oil slick in the Gulf has reached a beach in the United Arab Emirates, video from the AFP news agency showed on Tuesday, with experts warning it could threaten desalination plants as it spreads.
UAE authorities said Friday that they had "detected a tanker oil spill affecting Umm Al Quwain's beaches," referring to an emirate north of Dubai.
By Tuesday morning, footage shot by AFP showed workers cleaning up oil on the emirate's beaches, which had been shut earlier by authorities along with other beaches in the country.

Satellite images taken on Oct. 21 and analyzed by AFP show what appears to be a slick of about 70 square miles in that area. Three days later, images showed it had quadrupled in size to around 290 square miles.
Experts from NGOs including Dutch peace group PAX said oil came from the tanker GEM NO.2 after it was attacked on Oct. 9.
They warned the slick could affect operations at UAE desalination plants, crucial for supplying water to the Gulf country.

"Satellite imagery from October 26 shows oil slicks a few hundred metres away from the intake of the Naqaa desalination plant. It remains unclear to what extent this will affect the process at the plant itself," said Wim Zwijnenburg from PAX.
The British maritime security agency UKMTO reported on Oct. 9 that a vessel had been hit by a projectile off the UAE coast, causing a fire that was later brought under control.

Mohsen Rezaee, secretary of Iran's Supreme National Security Council, said regional countries should not rely on the United States for security, arguing that Washington has failed to provide credible security guarantees.

In a post on X Tuesday, Rezaee wrote: "America has not brought security to any country in the region, and Washington's inability to provide security guarantees has become clear. Security in West Asia must originate from within the region, and any foreign intervention must be prevented."
The U.S. has military bases in several Gulf countries that repeatedly were targeted at the height of the war.

A Houthi official said Tuesday that the Egyptian parliament's decision to authorize President Abdel Fattah el-Sisi to deploy forces to Saudi Arabia to help the kingdom defend against the Iran-backed group's attacks was a declaration of war.

"Egypt and its parliament declared support for what is called the defense of the Kingdom of Saudi Arabia, and in doing so, it declares war against the Republic of Yemen," said Mohammed Ali al-Houthi, a member of the Houthi political bureau, in a Telegram post.
El-Sisi stressed last week that the Egyptian deployment would be entirely defensive, "and does not include an attack on Yemen."

Oil prices held more or less steady early Tuesday, with international benchmark Brent crude hovering around $116 a barrel, little changed from the previous day when senior officials from Saudi Arabia, Turkey and Pakistan held talks with Iran in an attempt to stop the Middle East war from reigniting. Tehran said the discussions were "very good."
Officials from the three Mecca pact countries flew to Iran as part of efforts to "de-escalate between the parties to the current crisis," a Saudi foreign ministry statement said.

The talks followed warnings by the United States, Iran and Israel that hostilities could restart in the eight-month war, with some observers suggesting the period between next Tuesday's U.S. midterm elections and the new Congress taking office could be particularly fraught.
Also in view are elections in Israel, where voters began delivering their verdict on Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu, who told President Trump a week ago that they have "a job to finish" in Iran.
Israelis started casting votes Tuesday morning in a national election set to shape the country's next government, with the Iran war looming large over their decisions.

Israeli Defense Minister Israel Katz, echoing warnings issued repeatedly by Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu for weeks leading up to the vote, told voters that they were facing a decision "between two security paradigms: an approach based on offense, initiative, and decisive victory — or a return to a policy of containment and restraint."

"We have struck Iran twice and eliminated existential threats; we have expanded Israel's security perimeter in Lebanon, Syria, and Gaza to protect Israeli communities; and we are currently strengthening and fortifying our eastern border and the Jordan Valley," he said, calling on Israeli voters to "support this path in order to finish the job."
Netanyahu has called for Israel and the U.S. to resume attacks on Iran, telling President Trump, who has endorsed him enthusiastically, last week, "we have a job to finish."

The Iranian regime has dismissed the importance of the Israeli election, with foreign ministry spokesman Esmaeil Baqaei telling reporters Monday that the outcome will have no bearing on Iran's preparedness to face a resumption of hostilities, or to negotiate a deal to end the war based on its longstanding demands.
The Saudi-led coalition fighting Yemen's Houthi rebels said on Tuesday that it had shot down three missiles fired by the group toward the kingdom's eastern region.
"Air defenses intercepted and destroyed three ballistic missiles launched by the terrorist Houthi militia toward the Eastern Province," coalition spokesman Turki Al-Malki wrote on X.
Senior officials from Saudi Arabia, Turkey and Pakistan held talks with Iran on Monday in an attempt to stop the Middle East war from reigniting, with Tehran saying the discussions were "very good."

Officials from the three Mecca pact countries flew to Iran as part of efforts to "de-escalate between the parties to the current crisis," a Saudi foreign ministry statement said. It was the first joint visit to Tehran by Pakistan, Saudi Arabia and Turkey since they formed a defense alliance in Mecca, the holy city in western Saudi Arabia, in August.
The talks, which included heavyweight Saudi Defense Minister Prince Khalid bin Salman, followed warnings by the United States, Iran and Israel that hostilities could restart in the eight-month war.

The delegations met Iranian President Massoud Pezeshkian and Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi. The meeting ended without concrete announcements, with the various parties saying they "agreed to continue discussions" according to Iranian state media.

But Iran's security chief Mohsen Rezaei said the discussions in the capital were "very good," according to state television. "I feel that a new atmosphere is emerging in the region... I sensed a very positive atmosphere in the discussions among the gentlemen," said the head of Iran's Supreme National Security Council.

He said they agreed that security in the region "should be achieved by the countries themselves, and that we must prevent any kind of foreign intervention," saying emphasis was put on the Israeli occupation of southern Lebanon, southern Syria, Gaza and the West Bank.
Kuwait condemned three men to death on Monday for plotting the assassination of the deputy prime minister, collaborating with Iran and joining Hezbollah, two judiciary sources told AFP.
The three men are all from the Shia Muslim community, which makes up around a third of Kuwait's population.
Hussein Abdallah al-Maatouq, a religious dignitary and secretary-general of the National Islamic Alliance, was among the three condemned by the criminal court, the sources said.
Another of the trio had been convicted in 2016 of terrorism before being pardoned by the country's emir. He was arrested again in April, the sources said.

The men are accused of undermining national interests, collaborating with Iran, planning the assassination of the deputy prime minister and interior minister, and membership of Hezbollah, which is classified as a terrorist group by Kuwait.
The court sentenced 11 other people connected to the case to five years of hard labor.
Since the start of the Middle East war in February, Gulf countries, including Kuwait, have arrested dozens of people with suspected ties to Iran.
A vessel was on fire off the coast of Iraq on Monday, according to the U.K. Maritime Trade Operations center, or UKMTO, citing multiple third-party reports.
The vessel was situated 63 nautical miles from Al-Faw, a coastal town located along the Gulf between Iran and Kuwait, the maritime monitor said.
"Crew status, damage assessment, and environment impact are unknown," wrote UKMTO of the incident, which it deemed "suspicious activity."
The agency reminded those transiting the area to do so with caution while authorities investigate what may have occurred.
Wrapping up his re-election campaign on Monday, Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu claimed that Israel could face potential annihilation by Iran if his political rivals prevailed over him.

Over the course of a neck-and-neck race, Netanyahu has campaigned heavily on his security credentials, insisting only he can "finish the job" against Tehran and painting his main challenger, ex-army chief Gadi Eisenkot, as soft on Israel's sworn foe.

"I think this is a fateful moment for the future of the state, because we have enemies who want to annihilate us," Netanyahu told Israel's Channel 14 the day before Tuesday's vote, adding, "Gadi Eisenkot will not strike Iran."

Eisenkot has in turn accused the premier of playing politics with security on the election's eve and citing the Iran threat when it suits him — an allegation that came after a report, citing unnamed sources, said there were concerns within the Israeli army that the war was being politicized.
Netanyahu dismissed the report as "rubbish," and Defense Minister Israel Katz said any reports of a gap between the army and political leadership were "entirely baseless and false."

High-level delegations from Saudi Arabia, Pakistan and Turkey were in Tehran on Monday for meetings with Iranian authorities to try to avert renewed fighting in the Iran war, Iran's Foreign Ministry said. Iran and the three countries party to the Mecca defense pact — Saudi Arabia, Turkey and Pakistan — agreed to continue talks after a "first" meeting in Tehran, Iranian state television reported.

Saudi Defense Minister Khalid bin Salman, Pakistani army chief Field Marshal Asim Munir and Ibrahim Kalin, the head of Turkey's intelligence service, met with Iran's top security officials and negotiators to push for a deal between Tehran and Washington.

Iranian Foreign Ministry spokesperson Esmail Baghaei told reporters in Tehran that the agenda for the Monday meeting wasn't set, but the talks would "undoubtedly address the most pressing threats to regional security," while Saudi Arabia said in a statement that the delegations hoped to find "ways to de-escalate tensions, enhance regional security and promote its stability."

Two regional officials, who spoke on condition of anonymity because they weren't authorized to speak to reporters, told the Associated Press that the war in Yemen and strikes by Iran-backed Houthi rebels against Saudi Arabia were also among the topics discussed during the talks.

During the talks on Monday, Iranian President Masoud Pezeshkian said that Iran supports any agreement that would deepen regional cooperation, resolve differences and make greater use of the shared resources and capabilities of Islamic countries.

The meeting followed Qatari mediators' trip to Tehran on Sunday, which was coordinated alongside the U.S. and came as part of an effort to scale back regional tensions, a regional official, who spoke on condition of anonymity because of the sensitivity of the talks, told AP.

Russian President Vladimir Putin will hold five bilateral meetings with foreign leaders on the sidelines of the eighth summit of the Gas Exporting Countries Forum (GECF), including with Iranian President Masoud Pezeshkian and Qatari Emir Sheikh Tamim bin Hamad Al Thani, Kremlin aide Yuri Ushakov said Monday, according to Interfax.

Pezeshkian said before departing Tehran that his visit to Moscow would include discussions aimed at securing energy transit routes and eliminating insecurity in the Middle East, which he said was caused by the war sparked by the joint U.S.-Israeli assault on Iran almost eight months ago.

The Saudi-led coalition backing Yemen's government in the escalating civil war with the Iran-backed Houthis claimed Monday to have shot down three more drones over the Saudi capital Riyadh, and in the south of the country.
In a post on X, coalition spokesman Maj. Gen. Turki Al-Malki announced the "interception and destruction of 3 drones in the Riyadh region and the southern region."
He did not specify where the drones came from, but the Houthis have attacked Saudi Arabia with missiles and drones for weeks in retaliation for the kingdom's involvement in the Yemen war.

Earlier Monday, al-Malki said Saudi air defenses intercepted and destroyed a ballistic missile launched by the Houthis at Riyadh. The Saudis have struggled to intercept Houthi missiles and drones on the kingdom's infrastructure.
Israeli TV station Channel 12 reported Sunday that Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu had fallen out with army chief Eyal Zamir over an unspecified new directive on Iran.
Netanyahu and Defense Minister Israel Katz have both denied the reports, but a senior Israeli source with deep knowledge of the people involved has told CBS News the report of a rift seems credible.

The biggest tell, the source said, is that the Channel 12 report passed through military censorship. All stories by Israeli media that deal with national security must go through the censor before publication. This is key, according to the source, because it indicates that military brass felt it was necessary for the public to have the information before Israeli parliamentary elections on Tuesday.
Had it been false, the military censor would have simply prevented it from being published, the source told CBS News.

The other sign the report may be true is that Zamir, according to the source, is not personally opposed to renewed attacks on Iran – he's just opposed to the timing. The source said while there are likely new threats emerging from Iran, the question for commanders is whether new strikes need to happen now.
The military appears to believe that nothing requires a response within such a short timeframe, as Israelis prepare to cast their votes, according to the source.

Iranian President Masoud Pezeshkian said Monday that insecurity created by the United States in the Middle East was harming the entire world, as he prepared to travel to Moscow to attend the Gas Exporting Countries Forum (GECF) at the invitation of Russia's president Vladimir Putin.

Pezeshkian said the GECF has 12 member countries and, together with its eight observer members, oversees more than 70% of the world's gas supply. He added that a substantial share of the energy needed globally is exported by these nations.

"The problems the United States has created by igniting war in the region and bringing insecurity to Europe have disrupted the free flow of energy," Pezeshkian said, apparently referring to the ongoing U.S.-Iran war and Putin's long-standing claim that the U.S. and Europe are responsible for Russia's ongoing full-scale invasion of Ukraine.
He said his visit to Moscow would include discussions aimed at securing energy transit routes and eliminating insecurity.

Egypt's parliament on Monday approved a request by President Abdel Fattah el-Sisi that allows him to send troops to Saudi Arabia to help defend the kingdom from attacks by Yemen's Iran-backed Houthi rebels.
Egypt's House of Representatives "approved authorizing President Abdel Fattah el-Sisi to take the necessary measures to support the Kingdom of Saudi Arabia," state-run newspaper Al-Ahram reported.
El-Sisi stressed last week that it would only be a defensive mission, "and does not include an attack on Yemen."
Under Egypt's Constitution, the president must consult the National Defense Council and obtain approval from two-thirds of parliament before deploying the armed forces on a combat mission abroad.

Egypt has managed, so far, to stay out of the recent military conflicts across the Middle East and has been involved in some mediation efforts. Some in the country view that as one of el-Sisi's greatest achievements.
But political analyst Samir Ragheb, a retired army brigadier, told CBS News it was time for Egypt to make good on commitments to help secure the region.
"This is a time of war, not politics and statements," he said last week. "If Egypt fails to deliver on these promises, they will lose their meaning and amount to nothing more than empty threats."

The Saudi-led coalition backing Yemen's government said Monday that its forces carried out a military operation targeting areas controlled by the Iran-backed Houthi rebels in response to repeated attacks by the group using ballistic missiles and drones.
In a statement posted on X, coalition spokesman Maj. Gen. Turki Al-Malki said the operation sought to neutralize "the sources of threat," and included strikes against Houthi military infrastructure.
"The operation included the destruction of (5) tunnels used for storing ballistic missiles, (4) ballistic missile launchers, and a missile storage [unit]," Al-Malki said.
He added that the operation sought to disrupt supply lines between areas under Houthi control, targeting "fortifications, elements, and military equipment along the front lines inside Yemen."

Al-Malki said the operation was conducted in response to repeated Houthi attacks allegedly targeting civilians and civilian infrastructure in Saudi Arabia and Yemen. He said the coalition would continue taking "deterrent operational measures" to protect Saudi and Yemeni civilians.
He said the operation was conducted "in accordance with the Customary International Humanitarian Law."
Earlier, al-Malki said Saudi air defenses intercepted and destroyed a ballistic missile launched by the Houthis at the Saudi capital, Riyadh.

Iranian Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi has praised his nation's resilience after nearly eight months of war with the U.S., crediting civil defense efforts, national mobilization and cooperation between the armed forces and diplomatic service.

"The victorious resistance of our beloved country during the enemy's two recent acts of aggression has been made possible only through the solidarity and mobilization of all military and civilian sectors, as well as the proud presence of all segments of the Iranian people on the front lines of resistance," he said in a message marking Iran's Civil Defense Week.
Araghchi added that close coordination between the armed forces and the diplomatic service had brought "great achievements" in safeguarding Iran's independence and dignity.
He said the foreign ministry would use its diplomatic capabilities to defend the country politically and legally and protect national interests.
"It will spare no effort in pursuing this mission," Araghchi said.

Last week, intelligence firm Kpler told The Wall Street Journal that the shadow fleet of tankers holding Iran's offshore oil reserves, which it had been selling to China throughout the war against the U.S. and Israel, had run dry.

The millions of barrels of crude, held on dozens of oil tankers in Asian water, ran out in mid-October, Kpler told the outlet, with a U.S. naval blockade preventing Iran from replacing the crude being sold to Chinese refineries.
The U.S. naval blockade has cost Iran at least $25 billion in oil revenue, according to U.S. Central Command.
Iran's parliament speaker Mohammad Bagher Ghalibaf on Sunday called for a campaign to cut gas consumption by at least 10%, with officials anticipating shortages as winter approaches.
A tanker was struck in the Strait of Hormuz on Friday, the U.K. navy's Maritime Trade Operations center said Monday.
The maritime monitor said it received a "verified time-late report" of the incident, in which "a tanker transiting outbound was struck by an unknown projectile, disabling the vessel."
In a post on X, UKMTO said "the crew have been reported safe."

Iran claimed to have struck at least four tankers near the strait on Thursday last week, but there was no corroboration of its claims, and President Trump accused the Iranian regime of inventing attacks on commercial vessels in a bid to hike up global oil prices ahead of the U.S. midterm elections.

Defense Minister Israel Katz on Monday rejected reports of a rift between Israel's army and its civilian leaders - most notably Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu - over the prospect of new strikes in the war with Iran as "entirely baseless."
Israel's Channel 12 reported Sunday, citing unnamed sources, that there had been a confrontation between Netanyahu and army chief Eyal Zamir over an unspecified new directive.

Netanyahu dismissed the report as "rubbish" during a TV appearance, and Katz characterized it as an effort to cast doubt on the Netanyahu administration's judgment on the eve of close parliamentary elections that could unseat him.

"The reports about gaps between the political echelon and the IDF [army] on the Iran issue are entirely baseless and false," Katz said on X, insisting there was "complete" coordination between the two.

In its report, Channel 12 said Zamir had demanded a detailed discussion as well as legal guarantees and the signatures of the political leadership before carrying out the directive he had received. The outlet did not offer details of the purported directive, but cited sources saying there were concerns within the army that the war might be exploited for political gain.

The price of Brent crude oil hovered around $115 a barrel early Monday after surging at the end of last week over global supply concerns linked to the ongoing wars in the Middle East and Ukraine, as the northern hemisphere heads into the gas-hungry winter.
President Trump has fueled speculation that he could order a resumption of U.S. strikes on Iran after next Tuesday's midterm elections.
The president told Fox News on Sunday: "I have a decision to make: Do I finish it off, which would be very easy to do, or do I make a deal? That's all."

Additional U.S. forces, including a third aircraft carrier group, have been sent to the region, though U.S. diplomatic staffing levels have been reduced, and sources told CBS News last week that the overall American military footprint in the Middle East was also being quietly reduced.
Iran's foreign ministry said Monday that the outcome of the Israeli elections in which Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu is facing a tight race will make "no difference".

"It makes no difference to us who, in these elections, takes the helm of a regime that has brought nothing but violence and massacres to our region," said ministry spokesman Esmaeil Baqaei in a weekly press briefing, a day ahead of the Israeli legislative polls.
Netanyahu claimed Sunday that Israel had "intelligence signs that our enemies, Iran and its proxies, could challenge us with attacks in order to disrupt the elections."
Senior officials from Saudi Arabia, Turkey and Pakistan will hold talks on regional security with Iranian officials on Monday in Tehran, Iranian and Saudi authorities said.
The meeting will follow eight months of war in the Middle East and recent U.S. and Israeli threats of renewed attacks against Iran.

"As agreed, Saudi Defense Minister Khalid bin Salman, Pakistani army chief General Asim Munir and Turkish intelligence chief Ibrahim Kalin will participate in this meeting," said Ali Bagheri Kani, the deputy secretary of Iran's Supreme National Security Council.
In an interview with state television, Kani said the meeting will also include Iran's security chief, Mohsen Rezaei.
Saudi Deputy Minister for Public Diplomacy Dr. Rayed Krimly confirmed that the kingdom's defense minister was heading a delegation to Tehran on Monday.
"The visit comes as part of the continued efforts by the Makkah Joint Defense Agreement countries for de-escalation between parties involved in the ongoing crisis," Krimly said in a post on X.
It is aimed at "promoting dialogue and diplomatic solutions, in support of the mediation efforts carried out by the State of Qatar and the Islamic Republic of Pakistan," he added.

The Saudi-led military coalition fighting alongside the Yemeni government in the country's civil war said Monday it intercepted a ballistic missile fired by Yemen's Houthis, after the Iran-backed group claimed a new attack on the international airport in Riyadh.

A Houthi spokesperson said the group launched attacks on the airport on Sunday, just hours after it resumed flights. Deadly strikes by the rebel group earlier this month had forced the airport to shut down operations for more than two weeks .

Coalition spokesman Turki Al-Malki said on Monday that air defenses "intercepted and destroyed a ballistic missile" fired by the Houthis toward Riyadh and destroyed two ballistic missile launchers in Yemen's capital Sanaa.
Houthi military spokesman Yahya Saree said Monday the group "successfully targeted" the airport with a ballistic missile, and struck oil pumping stations with drones.
Saree previously warned that Riyadh airport was still "unsafe" and a "military target," as the airport prepared to resume international flights.
The airport closure was a major blow for Saudi Arabia, forcing the postponement of the kingdom's flagship investment conference until 2027 and disrupting travel plans for thousands of passengers.

Saudi Arabia and the government it backs in Yemen have come under sustained attack in recent weeks from the Houthis as a years-long truce broke down over the summer, shifting the focus of the wider U.S.-Iran war that erupted in February.
Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu said that Iran and its allies might try to disrupt Tuesday's Israeli elections, warning the Islamic republic against any hostile acts.
"The IDF is prepared in both defense and offense," Netanyahu said in a video released by his office on Sunday, using the acronym for the Israeli army.

"We have intelligence signs that our enemies, Iran and its proxies, could challenge us with attacks in order to disrupt the elections," he added. "Don't test us. You will suffer disproportionate blows."

President Trump said Sunday morning that he's deciding between reaching an agreement with Tehran and taking action to "finish them off," after suggesting Friday that Washington "may do another little Epic Fury," in reference to the U.S. and Israel's joint military campaign against Iran.
"Now, my question is, do I make a deal with them, or do I finish them off?" said Mr. Trump in an interview with Fox News' "Sunday Morning Futures."

He also claimed that the U.S. now controls the Strait of Hormuz and criticized former President Barack Obama for the Joint Comprehensive Plan of Action, or JCPOA, which is better known as the Iran nuclear deal. Obama signed the agreement in 2015, but Mr. Trump pulled out of it during his first term in office.
Iran's Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi said Sunday that a potential resumption of war with Israel and the United States would not change his country's positions.

The remarks came amid mounting tensions between Tehran and Washington after President Trump said Friday that Washington "may do another little Epic Fury," referring to the U.S.-Israeli campaign on Iran that began on Feb. 28.

"Recently, there has been talk of a new war, but I am already thinking about the post-war period. Whether there is war or not, our policies remain the same," said Araghchi during a televised event in Tehran.
"They have already done so twice and have seen the results. If they want to try again, they know they will achieve no different outcome from those of the past."

Direct negotiations between the U.S. and Iran have appeared to stall for weeks, but Iranian foreign ministry spokesperson Esmaeil Baqaei said earlier Sunday that Tehran had not closed the window of diplomacy and messages were still being passed to the U.S. via intermediaries.

notas.titulo: UFRJ debate recomposição orçamentária e impacto cambial na pesquisa
notas.texto: A Universidade Federal do Rio de Janeiro abriu nesta terça-feira a Semana do Servidor Público com painéis sobre a valorização do funcionalismo e a gestão das universidades federais. No Instituto de Biofísica Carlos Chagas Filho (IBCCF), pesquisadores e coordenadores de pós-graduação apontam preocupação com a recente volatilidade do dólar, que eleva custos de reagentes biológicos, enzimas e equipamentos de precisão cotados no exterior. A comunidade acadêmica da UFRJ aguarda o detalhamento do Projeto de Lei Orçamentária e a abertura dos editais de fomento à pesquisa prometidos para o novo mandato federal, além dos editais internos de mestrado e doutorado abertos para 2027.

Entre os tópicos centrais estão a carreira docente e técnica, a manutenção dos edifícios históricos e laboratórios, e os desafios da autonomia universitária frente ao cenário fiscal desenhado para 2027.

notas.texto: Reunidos em Bruxelas para sessões preparatórias do Conselho de Energia e Meio Ambiente, ministros da União Europeia debatem diretrizes comuns sobre descarbonização industrial e incentivos para fontes renováveis, visando a próxima cúpula climática global (COP31). De acordo com comunicado divulgado pelo Conselho da UE, o bloco busca acelerar a autonomia energética frente à instabilidade no mercado de hidrocarbonetos e aos riscos geopolíticos nas rotas marítimas do Oriente Médio. Entre os pontos centrais estão a fixação de padrões para hidrogênio verde e critérios mais rígidos de pegada de carbono para insumos importados, medidas que incidem diretamente sobre produtores e exportadores brasileiros.
